title: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
desc: Contrasts advocates’ refinement claims with critics’ concerns about retrospective adjustment and weak testing, especially in professional services.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns disruption as a specific causal theory, not whether industries change or newcomers sometimes win.
kps.d: Christensen, Raynor and McDonald define disruption as entry through overlooked low-end customers or previous nonconsumers, followed by improvement and mainstream adoption. They argue that customer priorities and resource-allocation routines can leave capable incumbents vulnerable. Major technological breakthroughs that serve existing customers can instead be sustaining innovations. Goldfarb accepts that industries undergo disruption but disputes Christensen’s mechanism; Lepore challenges its expansion into a general explanation of change.

qs.q: By contrast, new-market disruptions take hold in a completely new value network and appeal to customers who have previously gone without the product.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: It's just the mechanism does not work in the way Christensen has described."  Disruption theory serves as a "thinking shortcut" that obscures, rather than clarifies, why some firms thrive during periods of change, and others die, he says.
qs.a: The Myth of 'Disruptive Innovation' · Market & press · 2015

kps.k: The main quantitative critique finds weak conformity among the theory’s own historical examples, not a measured economy-wide failure rate.
kps.d: King and Baatartogtokh’s review asked 79 experts to assess 77 claimed examples against four elements: sustaining innovation, overshooting customer needs, incumbent capability to respond, and subsequent incumbent difficulties. They counted expert disagreements in the theory’s favor. Institutional accounts report that only 9% met all four elements and that incumbents survived or thrived in 39%. These accounts describe the same study, not independent replications. The supplied article capture lacks the full results section, and the findings test historical case conformity rather than prospective forecasting accuracy.

qs.q: In it, King and co-author Baljir Baartartogtokh surveyed 79 experts on 77 examples of disruption claimed by Christensen.
qs.a: Deflating Disruption Theory · Market & press · 2015

qs.q: If multiple experts on the same case disagreed on the answer to a question, we gave the benefit of the doubt to the theory of disruption, and agreement with that element of the theory of disruption was judged confirmed.
qs.a: How Useful Is the Theory of Disruptive Innovation? · Academia · 2015

kps.k: Advocates describe theoretical refinement and predictive value; critics see retrospective adjustment and insufficiently demanding tests.
kps.d: Christensen and co-authors claim cross-industry validation and improved prediction of fledgling-business success, but the supplied passages give no test designs or effect sizes. They present the distinction between low-end and new-market entry as a response to anomalies. Goldfarb argues that selective cases and adjustments after the event impede refutation, and calls for systematic cross-industry predictive tests. Lepore contrasts Christensen’s 2007 prediction of iPhone failure with its reported $150 billion revenue over five years. The 2015 restatement classifies the original iPhone as sustaining within smartphones and its subsequent internet-access model as disruptive to laptops, illustrating the debate over market boundaries and retrospective classification.

qs.q: But there is cause for hope: Empirical tests show that using disruptive theory makes us measurably and significantly more accurate in our predictions of which fledgling businesses will succeed.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: A valid way to explore the theory's universality, he added, "would be to take several industries based upon certain criteria — say, high tech, low tech, manufacturing and services — and then explore the predictive validity of the theory of disruption across these industries.
qs.a: The Myth of 'Disruptive Innovation' · Market & press · 2015

kps.k: Alternative explanations challenge any simple equation between incumbent experience, inertia and failure.
kps.d: The Myth of 'Disruptive Innovation' reports King and Tucci’s 2002 finding that experienced disk-drive firms were more likely to enter new markets. Goldfarb also questions whether incumbents always possess realistic response capabilities and attributes Fuji’s resilience to diversification. Lepore’s Bucyrus reassessment points to continued growth, economic shocks and a leveraged buyout rather than a straightforward technological-displacement story. The outsider-innovation literature offers a distinct, qualified mechanism: freedom from established assumptions may aid creativity, while some expertise remains valuable. That literature-based proposition does not establish Christensen’s market trajectory or predict entrant success.

qs.q: Tucci found in a 2002 paper, disk-drive firms with the most experience in existing markets were actually more likely to enter new ones.) But Christensen has in the years since suggested that the theory is a sort of universal explanation for technological shifts.
qs.a: The Myth of 'Disruptive Innovation' · Market & press · 2015

qs.q: (Caterpillar sustained heavy losses, too.) In the early nineteen-nineties, after a disastrous leveraged buyout handled by Goldman Sachs, Bucyrus entered Chapter 11 protection, but it made some sizable acquisitions when it emerged, as Bucyrus International, and was a leading maker of mining equipment, just as it had been a century earlier.
qs.a: The Disruption Machine: What the Gospel of Innovation Gets Wrong · Market & press · 2014

kps.k: Professional-service applications identify plausible competitive pressures but do not establish inevitable legal-sector displacement.
kps.d: In 2013, Christensen, Wang and van Bever argued that technology, alternative staffing, wider data access and more sophisticated clients were eroding consulting and law firms’ historical protections of opacity and agility. They cited a fall in classic strategy work from 60–70% to about 20% over the preceding 30 years and an AdvanceLaw survey in which 72% of general counsel intended to move more work away from white-shoe firms. The survey measures intentions, not completed migration. Their claim that every industry eventually faces disruption extends beyond these observations, and they acknowledge uncertainty about consulting’s trajectory. Rise of the Robot Lawyers? reports applications of the theory to law without supplying evidence of predictive success or lawyer displacement.

qs.q: But at traditional strategy-consulting firms, the share of work that is classic strategy has sharply declined over the past 30 years, from 60% or 70% to only about 20%.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

qs.q: Numerous acolytes have sought to apply his theory to the law.
qs.a: Rise of the Robot Lawyers? · Academia · 2019

kps.k: The practical debate favors context-sensitive responses over an unconditional imperative to disrupt.
kps.d: Christensen and co-authors recommend maintaining profitable core operations and sustaining investment while exploring a disruptive model in a separate, protected division. They acknowledge that this structure sometimes fails, entrant success is not guaranteed, and complete substitution may take decades or never occur. King and Baatartogtokh likewise reject wholesale abandonment of the theory, recommending its useful elements alongside classical strategic analysis. Lepore’s examples of costly reinvention challenge disruption as a survival imperative, but do not establish a general rule against innovation.

qs.q: Incumbent companies do need to respond to disruption if it’s occurring, but they should not overreact by dismantling a still-profitable business.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: Morrison-Knudsen announced in 1995 that it had lost three hundred and fifty million dollars, by which point the company had essentially collapsed—not because it didn’t disruptively innovate but because it did.
qs.a: The Disruption Machine: What the Gospel of Innovation Gets Wrong · Market & press · 2014

kps.k: A separate boundary dispute asks whether commercial disruption provides an appropriate standard for public-serving institutions.
kps.d: Lepore distinguishes novelty from improvement and argues that education, health care, museums and journalism carry obligations beyond earnings. Her criticism concerns both transferring a business theory across unlike domains and treating upheaval as inherently desirable. She interprets disruption’s popularity through marketing and fear; Goldfarb points to publication-derived authority and intellectual investment in theories. These are attributed explanations of the theory’s reception, not independent proof that its mechanism fails. The practical implication is to assess institutional outcomes and duties separately from entrant growth or commercial success.

qs.q: Replacing “progress” with “innovation” skirts the question of whether a novelty is an improvement: the world may not be getting better and better but our devices are getting newer and newer.
qs.a: The Disruption Machine: What the Gospel of Innovation Gets Wrong · Market & press · 2014

qs.q: "It becomes a fact."  Then there's the sociological problem that people who know the theory best become invested in defending it, rather than challenging it.
qs.a: The Myth of 'Disruptive Innovation' · Market & press · 2015

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources are substantively divided on the proposition. King and Baatartogtokh support it through a structured historical-case review reporting that only 9% of Christensen’s claimed examples met all four elements, while still treating disruption theory as selectively useful alongside other strategic approaches. By contrast, Christensen, Raynor and McDonald oppose the proposition’s assessment of weak empirical support: they claim validation across many industries and improved predictive accuracy, although the supplied material gives no test designs or effect sizes. Christensen, Wang and van Bever likewise extend the theory confidently to professional services, treating observed competitive pressures and buyer intentions as signs of disruption despite uncertainty about its exact path. Other research neither resolves this empirical dispute nor fits neatly on either side: the outsider-innovation source redirects attention to cognitive distance from established assumptions, and Rise of the Robot Lawyers? merely reports the theory and its application to law without testing it. Thus, within this curated selection—not as a measure of the wider academic field—the principal division is between demands for systematic historical and predictive validation and advocates’ claims that a narrowly defined, refined theory already has cross-industry explanatory value.

qs.q: They found that only nine percent of Christensen’s 77 cases actually matched all the elements of Christensen’s own theory.
qs.a: How Useful Is the Theory of Disruptive Innovation? · Academia · 2015

qs.q: The key elements of that theory have been tested and validated through studies of many industries, including retail, computers, printing, motorcycles, cars, semiconductors, cardiovascular surgery, management education, financial services, management consulting, cameras, communications, and computer-aided design software.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources support the cluster’s principal proposition. Across the sources, the common argument is not that industries never change or entrants never defeat incumbents, but that Christensen’s specific causal theory has been accepted and extended more broadly than its evidence warrants. They point to weak conformity among the theory’s own historical cases, questionable case selection and interpretation, retrospective recalibration, limited prospective testing, and plausible alternative explanations for incumbent outcomes. Material variation lies in the remedy and scope of criticism: the Smith Brain Trust account foregrounds Goldfarb’s methodological challenge and demand for systematic cross-industry predictive testing; the Tuck article adopts a more reformist position, retaining useful elements of disruption theory alongside classical strategy; and Lepore advances the broadest critique, adding historical counterexamples, failed prediction, circular classification, and objections to transferring a commercial framework to public-serving institutions. These sources therefore converge on the synthesis’s evidentiary caution while differing over whether disruption theory should be narrowed and supplemented or treated as a substantially unreliable general account of change. Because this is a curated selection, that convergence should not be taken as representative of all market analysts, consultancies or press commentary.

qs.q: They found that only nine percent of Christensen’s 77 cases actually matched all the elements of Christensen’s own theory.
qs.a: Deflating Disruption Theory · Market & press · 2015

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources divide sharply over the proposition. Christensen, Wang and van Bever oppose it by treating disruption as a universal eventual threat and interpreting changes in professional services—technology, alternative staffing, wider data access, more sophisticated clients and intended movement of legal work away from white-shoe firms—as signs that disruption is already under way. Their acknowledgement that consulting’s precise trajectory cannot be forecast limits the certainty of timing, but not their confidence in the theory’s broad applicability. Lepore supports the proposition by disputing the historical evidence, prospective predictive record and retrospective classification used to validate disruption theory. She also argues that industry change and business failure do not by themselves establish Christensen’s specific mechanism, and that disruption should not become an unconditional prescription, particularly for public-serving institutions. Thus, the period supplies both an assertive professional-services application and a foundational methodological critique; the shared recognition that institutions and markets change does not resolve whether disruption theory reliably explains or predicts that change. These curated sources demonstrate an internal dispute, not the prevalence of either view among pre-2015 commentators.

qs.q: If our long study of disruption has led us to any universal conclusion, it is that every industry will eventually face it.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

elens.an: The period’s evidence overall supports the proposition that disruption theory’s historical examples weakly fit its claimed predictions. The strongest basis is King and Baatartogtokh’s review: despite resolving expert disagreement in the theory’s favour, only 9% of 77 claimed cases reportedly met all four defining elements. Goldfarb and reporting on the study reinforce this critique by distinguishing real industrial change from Christensen’s specific mechanism, questioning selective case construction and retrospective recalibration, and calling for systematic cross-industry predictive testing. This support is qualified rather than dismissive: the critics recommend retaining useful, context-specific elements alongside other strategic approaches. Material internal variation remains. Christensen, Raynor and McDonald oppose the central empirical assessment by claiming validation across many industries and significantly improved predictions, while narrowing the theory’s definition and acknowledging that it neither guarantees entrant success nor explains business success generally. The outsider-innovation source redirects attention to cognitive distance from entrenched assumptions, and the legal-automation excerpt merely reports applications to law without testing them. Because the corpus is curated and some supporting accounts repeat the same underlying study, source numbers do not indicate wider prevalence or independent replication.
